_comment: Reusable permission rules. Merge into a project's .claude/settings.json permissions block. deny is what may never happen; allow is this repository's own gates, which otherwise depend on the auto-mode classifier deciding the same command the same way twice. No allow rule here may match an invocation that writes: the two generators are named at their --check form exactly, because a trailing wildcard — with or without a space before it — also matches the bare command, and the bare command is the writing one.
_anchoring_comment: What a Bash deny rule binds is a spelling, and the spelling is matched per subcommand rather than per Bash call: the harness splits a compound command on `&&`, `||`, `;`, `|`, `|&`, `&` and newlines and matches every rule against each piece independently, and it unwraps a fixed set of command wrappers. Probed rather than read off the documentation, because the two disagree — `git push --force ...`, `echo probe && git push --force ...` and `timeout 5 git push --force ...` were all refused, while `FOO=bar git push --force ...`, `sh -c '...'` and a loop body all ran. Two of those lines are where the documentation and the machine disagree, so read both as measured rather than as promised. The platform documents a deny rule as matching past a leading environment assignment, and on the machine this was probed on it does not. It also documents `command` as a stripped wrapper, and `command git push --force ...` escaped, while `timeout` — documented the same way — was refused. Treat an env-prefixed spelling and a wrapper you have not tried as unbound until your own probe says otherwise; re-run these rather than trusting the list. So what escapes is not everything after the first word — it is a command the matcher never sees as a plain subcommand: an env-assignment prefix, a loop body, an `sh -c` string, an exec wrapper it does not know. Narrower than a typo, wider than nothing. A pattern with a leading `*` does reach a loop body — probed — but it matches the words wherever they stand, so it refuses every commit message, issue body and search that names the verb, and none is used here. The one case that would be unrecoverable is bound elsewhere and not here: a force-push to the default branch is refused by the repository's own branch protection, server-side, with no bypass actor, where no local spelling reaches it. That is where a guarantee of that class belongs; a deny list is not, and saying so is the point of this note.
_classes_comment: Severity classes for the drift report, most severe first. Read by hooks/permissions-check.sh and by nothing else; not part of the settings schema, and not merged into a project. `match` holds literal prefixes of a rule's own text — this classifies strings in the list below, it never matches a command, so it is not a second copy of the platform's permission matcher and cannot drift into one. A rule matching no class is still reported, last, under `other`: the ranking exists to raise what matters and must never be able to hide anything. The classes earned their order from a real install that carried the three `gh` rules missing while the report emitted 67 entries flat, whose first thirty were enumerated `git checkout` path variants.
